title: One malformed receipt permanently breaks GET /receipts and MCP list_receipts (TypeError not caught)
scenario: Any token holder, or a buggy app build, POSTs {"schema":1,"model":{"id":"m"},"workloads":5} (or workloads true/3.2). save() only checks schema==1, so it stores the receipt (201). Every later GET /receipts that reaches that file (no filter, or a matching model filter) runs `for w in r.get("workloads") or []` and raises TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable. list() only catches OSError/JSONDecodeError, handle() only catches Overflow/Lookup/ValueError, and jobworker._route only catches ValueError/JSONDecodeError. The exception escapes the handler thread and the connection drops with no response. Receipts are never deleted, so the listing and the MCP list_receipts tool stay broken until someone removes the file by hand.
evidence: I reproduced it in a trial merge (integration+bench) with ReceiptStore directly. POST returned (201, {...}) and the listing then raised `TypeError 'int' object is not iterable`. GET of that one receipt still returned 200.
fix: Validate the shape in save(): workloads must be a list of dicts, model/device/load must be dicts when present, and string fields are bounded. In list(), also wrap summarize() in try/except (TypeError, AttributeError, ValueError) and skip bad files.
notes: UPHELD(high): I confirmed this by reading the code at origin/bench. In worker/receipts.py, save() checks only the size, that the body is JSON, that it is a dict, and that schema==1. A body like {"schema":1,"model":{"id":"m"},"workloads":5} is written to disk and returns 201. In summarize() (around line 38), the loop `for w in r.get("workloads") or []` evaluates `5 or []` to 5, so iterating raises TypeError: 'int' object is not iterable. The same happens with true or 3.2. The isinstance(w, dict) guard sits inside the loop, so it never runs. ReceiptStore.list() catches only (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError) around json.loads, and summarize() is called outside that try. receipts.handle() catches only OverflowError, LookupError and ValueError. federated.make_router passes /receipts straight to receipts_handle with no wrapper. jobworker Handler._route catches only (ValueError, json.JSONDecodeError). The TypeError therefore reaches BaseHTTPRequestHandler, which drops the connection with no response. mcp_bridge.t_list_receipts calls GET /receipts, so the MCP list_receipts tool fails the same way. The module docstring says receipts are never deleted by the worker, so every unfiltered listing, and every listing filtered to the bad receipt's model, keeps failing while that file is within the newest `limit` entries (newest first, so it always is right after upload). Medium severity is fair: any token holder can trigger it, it causes no data loss, and deleting the file by hand recovers. GET /receipts/{name} is unaffected, which matches the claim. | fix: In save(), reject the receipt with ValueError when workloads is present but not a list, or when model, device or load is present but not a dict. In list(), wrap `out.append(summarize(path.name, r))` in `try/except (TypeError, AttributeError, ValueError): continue`. Also make summarize() defensive: `wl = r.get("workloads"); wl = wl if isinstance(wl, list) else []`.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute the claim, and the code on origin/bench confirms it. save() only checks that the receipt parses to a dict with schema == 1. It never checks the type of `workloads`. summarize() (receipts.py ~line 38) runs `for w in r.get("workloads") or []`, and that line raises TypeError for any truthy value that is not iterable, such as 5, true or 3.2. The isinstance(w, dict) check sits inside the loop, so it never runs in that case. Nothing up the call stack catches TypeError: list() catches only (OSError, JSONDecodeError), handle() catches only Overflow/Lookup/ValueError (TypeError is not a ValueError subclass), federated.make_router passes /receipts straight to receipts_handle with no wrapper, and jobworker._route catches only (ValueError, JSONDecodeError). The exception therefore reaches BaseHTTPRequestHandler. socketserver prints the traceback and drops the connection without sending a response. The server itself keeps running, but every unfiltered or matching-model GET /receipts fails, and so does the MCP list_receipts call, which goes through the same endpoint (mcp_bridge.t_list_receipts). The module says receipts are never deleted, so this lasts until someone removes the file by hand. Reaching the endpoint needs a token, which keeps severity at medium. Other summarize fields are guarded: model and device go through isinstance, and `load` is passed through as-is. Only the workloads loop crashes. | fix: In summarize(), use `ws = r.get("workloads"); for w in (ws if isinstance(ws, list) else []):`. Also have save() reject a non-list `workloads` with a ValueError, which handle() returns as 400. Optionally, in list(), wrap summarize() in try/except (TypeError, AttributeError) and skip that file, so one bad file cannot break the listing.

UPHELD(high): I tried to refute this and could not; it reproduces. On origin/bench, worker/receipts.py save() only checks that the body is a JSON object with schema==1, so {"schema":1,"model":{"id":"m"},"workloads":5} is stored and returns 201. summarize() then runs `for w in r.get("workloads") or []` (about line 38). With an int, a float, or `true` that loop raises TypeError, because the `or []` fallback only covers falsy values. The guards on model and device are type-checked, but the guard on workloads is not.

Nothing on the path catches the error. ReceiptStore.list() catches only OSError and JSONDecodeError. receipts.handle() catches only Overflow, Lookup and Value errors. federated.make_router passes the call straight through. jobworker._route catches only ValueError and JSONDecodeError. The exception escapes the HTTP handler, the connection drops with no response, and MCP list_receipts fails.

The file is never deleted. list() sorts newest first and returns once `limit` receipts are collected, so the bad file breaks every unfiltered or model-matching listing until it is pushed past the limit by newer receipts or removed by hand. Fetching that one receipt with GET /receipts/{name} still works.

I reproduced it outside the repo with python -I against the bench copy of receipts.py: POST returned (201, ...), then GET /receipts raised TypeError 'int' object is not iterable.

Severity medium is fair: it needs a token holder or a buggy client, and it is a denial of service on the listing with no data loss. Strings or dicts passed as `workloads` do not crash, because non-dict items are skipped. | fix: In summarize(), replace the loop source with `ws = r.get("workloads"); ws = ws if isinstance(ws, list) else []`. In list(), wrap the summarize/_model_id step in try/except Exception and skip the bad file. Optionally, have save() reject receipts whose workloads is not a list of objects, returning 400.

title: UTF-16/32 or BOM-prefixed receipt is accepted, then poisons listing (400) or becomes unreadable
ref: origin/bench:worker/receipts.py save() json.loads(raw) vs get()/list() read_text(encoding='utf-8')
scenario: json.loads(bytes) auto-detects UTF-16, UTF-32 and UTF-8-with-BOM, so save() accepts such a body and stores the raw bytes. get() and list() decode with read_text(encoding='utf-8'). For UTF-16, list() raises UnicodeDecodeError, which it does not catch, so every GET /receipts returns 400 "'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff" from then on and list_receipts is dead. For a UTF-8 BOM, the receipt silently drops out of listings and GET /receipts/<name> returns 400. Bare NaN/Infinity is also accepted and re-emitted as non-standard JSON to clients.
evidence: Reproduced. utf16: POST 201, then list -> 400 {"error": "'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff ..."}, get -> 400. bom: POST 201, the listing shows only the other receipt, get -> 400. nan: POST 201 and the listing JSON contains NaN.
fix: In save(), decode explicitly: `text = raw.decode('utf-8')` (reject a BOM), then `json.loads(text, parse_constant=reject)`. Store canonical `json.dumps(receipt).encode()` instead of the raw bytes. In list(), also catch UnicodeDecodeError/ValueError.
notes:
UPHELD(high): I confirmed this on origin/bench:worker/receipts.py.

- **What save() accepts and stores.** save() calls json.loads(raw) on the raw bytes, and json.loads on bytes detects UTF-16, UTF-32 and a UTF-8 BOM. It then writes the raw bytes unchanged with tmp.write_bytes(raw).
- **Why list() breaks.** list() reads with path.read_text(encoding='utf-8') and catches only (OSError, json.JSONDecodeError). On a UTF-16 file the read raises UnicodeDecodeError, which escapes the loop. UnicodeDecodeError is a subclass of ValueError, so handle() returns 400.
- **Why get() breaks.** get() does the same read and returns 400 for that receipt.
- **The BOM case.** read_text keeps the BOM as U+FEFF, and json.loads(str) then raises JSONDecodeError ("Unexpected UTF-8 BOM"). The listing skips that receipt silently, and get() returns 400.
- **Why it doesn't clear.** The docstring says the worker never rewrites or deletes receipts, so one bad POST breaks GET /receipts until someone removes the file by hand.

I reproduced it with the file copied to a temp dir outside the repo. Saving a valid receipt, then a UTF-16 encoded one, made handle GET ['receipts'] return (400, "'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0") and GET of that receipt return the same 400.

The NaN part is minor; the persistent listing outage is the real defect. Medium severity is reasonable. | fix: In save(): decode with text = raw.decode('utf-8') and treat UnicodeDecodeError, or text starting with '﻿', as a 400. Then parse with json.loads(text, parse_constant=...), where the hook raises ValueError so NaN/Infinity are rejected. Store json.dumps(receipt, allow_nan=False).encode('utf-8') instead of the raw bytes. In list(), also catch UnicodeDecodeError/ValueError so files already on disk can't break the listing.

UPHELD(high): I checked this against the code on origin/bench (worker/receipts.py) and could not refute it.

1. save() calls json.loads(raw) on the raw bytes. Python detects UTF-16 and UTF-32 bytes and strips a UTF-8 BOM, so a UTF-16 body with schema 1 is accepted. save() then writes those raw bytes to disk with tmp.write_bytes(raw).
2. list() reads each file with read_text(encoding='utf-8') and catches only OSError and json.JSONDecodeError. I confirmed locally that the UnicodeDecodeError raised for UTF-16 bytes is not an OSError and not a JSONDecodeError. So the error escapes the loop. It is a ValueError, so handle() turns it into a 400 on every GET /receipts.
3. The module docstring says receipts are never deleted, and the API has no delete route. One bad upload therefore breaks the listing permanently until someone removes the file by hand.
4. A UTF-8 BOM body decodes to text starting with '﻿'. json.loads(str) then raises JSONDecodeError ("Unexpected UTF-8 BOM"). list() skips that receipt silently and get() returns 400.
5. NaN and Infinity are accepted because json.loads allows them by default.

Nothing upstream guards against this: save() does no encoding check, and handle() passes the raw body straight through. The iPad app sends UTF-8 JSON, so a normal client will not trigger it. A malformed or hostile POST will, which makes the claimed medium severity reasonable. | fix: In save(), decode the bytes as strict UTF-8 first: `text = raw.decode('utf-8')`, and raise ValueError on UnicodeDecodeError or on a leading '﻿'. Then parse with `json.loads(text, parse_constant=_reject)`, where _reject raises ValueError for NaN/Infinity. Store canonical bytes, `json.dumps(receipt, allow_nan=False).encode('utf-8')`, instead of raw. In list(), widen the except to `(OSError, ValueError)` so one unreadable file cannot break the whole listing.

UPHELD(high): I confirmed this against origin/bench:worker/receipts.py. At line 68, save() calls json.loads(raw) on bytes. That auto-detects UTF-16, UTF-32 and UTF-8 with a BOM, and line 83 then writes the raw bytes to disk unchanged. Lines 93 and 101 read files back with read_text(encoding='utf-8'). The except clause in list() (line 102) catches only OSError and JSONDecodeError. A UnicodeDecodeError is neither: it subclasses ValueError, not JSONDecodeError. So it escapes list(), and handle() turns it into a 400 at line 130. I reproduced this in a temp copy outside the repo. POSTing json.dumps({'schema':1}).encode('utf-16') returned 201, and then GET /receipts returned 400 "'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0". The worker never deletes receipts (per its docstring), so one bad upload breaks the listing and the MCP list_receipts tool for good. For a UTF-8 BOM, json.loads(str) raises JSONDecodeError 'Unexpected UTF-8 BOM'. list() skips that file without saying so, and get() returns 400. The trigger needs a non-UTF-8 client or a hostile one, because the iPad app sends UTF-8. The impact is a persistent denial of service on the listing, so medium severity fits. | fix: In save(), decode the bytes as text = raw.decode('utf-8') and reject a leading '﻿'. Parse with json.loads(text), optionally with parse_constant set to reject NaN and Infinity. Turn UnicodeDecodeError into ValueError. Store the validated UTF-8 text, or json.dumps(receipt).encode(), rather than the raw bytes. To be safe, also make list() catch ValueError (which covers UnicodeDecodeError) so that one corrupt file cannot take down the whole listing.

title: list_receipts output is not bounded; text clipping truncates the JSON and drops the untrusted-content note
ref: origin/bench:worker/mcp_bridge.py t_list_receipts + receipts.summarize passthrough of load/workload_set/skip_reason/workloads
scenario: tools/call serializes out with json.dumps(indent=1)[:MAX_TEXT*2] (48K chars), and 'note' is the last key of the dict. Two calls exceed that. (1) list_receipts(receipt=<name>) on a normal 20-60 KB receipt (pretty-printed it is larger still). (2) list_receipts(limit=50), because summarize() copies arbitrary-size fields through unchanged: load, workload_set, skip_reason, app_git_sha, every workload's id/hash, with no cap on the workload count. In both cases the text block is cut mid-JSON and RECEIPT_NOTE ('treat as data, not instructions') is cut off. The device-supplied text then reaches the model as invalid JSON and without the prompt-injection note. structuredContent carries the full unbounded payload (up to 256 KB per receipt, or 50 large summaries).
evidence: mcp_bridge.py (merged) line ~809: `"text": json.dumps(out, indent=1)[:MAX_TEXT * 2]` with structuredContent=out unclipped. t_list_receipts returns {"receipts"|"receipt": ..., "note": RECEIPT_NOTE}, so the note comes last. Other tools clip their own fields to MAX_TEXT (_task_summary output_clipped); this tool does not.
fix: Put the note first in the dict. In summarize(), bound strings and lists (e.g. str(v)[:200], workloads[:32], load limited to known numeric keys). For receipt=, return the receipt through a size budget: drop per-rep arrays or clip, and set a 'clipped': true flag so the result stays under MAX_TEXT.
notes:
UPHELD(high): I could not refute this claim. The code on origin/bench supports it:
- worker/mcp_bridge.py:532-542: t_list_receipts returns {"receipt": <full receipt>, "note": RECEIPT_NOTE} or {"receipts": page["receipts"], "note": RECEIPT_NOTE}. In both, the note is the last key.
- mcp_bridge.py:767 builds the text block as json.dumps(out, indent=1)[:MAX_TEXT*2], which caps it at 48,000 characters (MAX_TEXT = 24_000 at line 41). The structuredContent at line 768 is the same dict, not clipped.
- receipts.py ReceiptStore.get returns the whole stored receipt with json.loads and does not limit its size. save() accepts up to MAX_RECEIPT = 256 KB and only checks that it is a JSON object with schema == 1.
- The summarize() docstring itself says "the full receipt can be ~20-60 KB". A 60 KB receipt is already past the 48K cut before pretty-printing, and indent=1 makes it bigger.
- So list_receipts(receipt=name) on a normal large receipt returns JSON cut off mid-structure, and the untrusted-data note never appears in the text.

summarize() also copies load, workload_set, skip_reason and app_git_sha through as-is, and it does not cap how many workloads it lists. With limit=50, a few large receipts, or many workloads each, can also push the text past 48K.

Unlike _task_summary, this tool does not clip its own fields. Clients that read only content[].text see invalid JSON with the prompt-injection note missing. Medium severity is fair: the text loses data and a safety label, but it does not crash. | fix: Put the "note" key first in both return dicts of t_list_receipts. Then bound the output:
- For receipt=<name>: serialize the receipt. If it exceeds MAX_TEXT, drop the bulky per-rep arrays (or return summarize(name, r) plus "clipped": true) so the text stays valid JSON.
- In summarize(): clip string fields (for example str(v)[:200] for skip_reason, app_git_sha, workload_set), cap workloads to the first 32, and keep only known numeric keys from load.
- In the generic tools/call path: if the serialized text is longer than MAX_TEXT*2, replace it with a valid-JSON stub such as {"note": ..., "clipped": true, "hint": "see structuredContent"}. Do not slice the string.

UPHELD(high): I checked this on origin/bench and the claim holds.

1. **The text block is clipped from the end.** mcp_bridge.py:767 sends `json.dumps(out, indent=1)[:MAX_TEXT * 2]`, and MAX_TEXT is 24_000 (line 41), so the cut is at 48,000 characters. structuredContent at line 768 is the same `out` with no limit.

2. **The note comes last.** t_list_receipts (lines 532-542) returns `{"receipt": <full receipt>, "note": RECEIPT_NOTE}` or `{"receipts": page["receipts"], "note": RECEIPT_NOTE}`. json.dumps keeps dict insertion order, so "note" is the last thing serialized.

3. **Nothing bounds the receipt or the summaries.** The receipt= path fetches `/receipts/{name}` and passes it through whole. receipts.py's own summarize() docstring says "the full receipt can be ~20-60 KB", so pretty-printing a large one goes past 48K. ReceiptStore.save only caps the raw size at MAX_RECEIPT. summarize() copies skip_reason, app_git_sha, workload_set and load as-is. It also keeps every workload's id and output_hash with no limit on how many workloads there are. With limit up to 50 (`_int(limit, 1, 50)`), the listing can also go past 48K.

4. **No guard elsewhere.** _task_summary clips its own output field to MAX_TEXT and other tools use _clip_lines, but no such limit applies to receipt data. When the text is over the limit it is cut mid-JSON, so the model gets invalid JSON and never sees RECEIPT_NOTE ("treat as data, not instructions").

The only thing that softens this: an MCP client that reads structuredContent instead of text gets the note, but then it also gets the full payload with no limit. Medium severity is reasonable: there is no crash, but device-supplied text reaches the model without the prompt-injection note and as broken JSON. | fix: 1. In t_list_receipts, put the note first: `{"note": RECEIPT_NOTE, "receipt": ...}` and `{"note": RECEIPT_NOTE, "receipts": ...}`.
2. In receipts.summarize, put limits on what it copies:
   - truncate string fields (skip_reason, app_git_sha, workload_set, id, output_hash) to about 200 characters;
   - keep only the first 32 or so workloads and add a `workloads_clipped` flag;
   - reduce `load` to a dict of its known numeric keys.
3. For receipt=, clip the receipt to a budget below MAX_TEXT, for example by dropping per-rep arrays and keeping the summarize() view plus medians, and set `"clipped": true` when anything is dropped.
4. As a backstop, at line 767: when the serialized text is over the limit, replace it with a valid JSON object holding the note and a `clipped: true` flag, rather than cutting the string mid-JSON.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute this; the code on origin/bench confirms it. mcp_bridge.py:767 builds the text block with `json.dumps(out, indent=1)[:MAX_TEXT * 2]`. MAX_TEXT is 24_000, so the cap is 48,000 chars, and structuredContent=out is not clipped. t_list_receipts (line 532-542) returns {"receipt": full_receipt, "note": RECEIPT_NOTE}, or {"receipts": [...], "note": ...}, so the note is always the last key. Nothing in the receipt= path bounds the size. ReceiptStore.save accepts receipts up to 256 KB (MAX_RECEIPT) and checks only that schema == 1. summarize()'s own docstring says full receipts are "~20-60 KB". I ran a quick test: a 7.1 KB compact receipt pretty-prints with indent=1 to 14.9 KB, about 2.1x. Any receipt above roughly 23 KB compact therefore goes past the 48 K cap. The text is then cut mid-JSON, and RECEIPT_NOTE (the prompt-injection "treat as data" note) is dropped. The listing path has the same problem: summarize() copies load, workload_set, skip_reason, app_git_sha and every workload's id/output_hash through unbounded, with no cap on workload count, and up to 50 summaries. Device-supplied content can therefore push the note out of the text block. The impact is invalid JSON and a missing injection note in the text content, but no crash, so medium severity fits. | fix: In t_list_receipts, put "note" first in the returned dict. Python dicts keep insertion order, so the note serializes first and survives clipping. In receipts.summarize(), clip string fields (e.g. str(v)[:200]), cap workloads (e.g. [:32]) and reduce load to known numeric keys. For receipt=, apply a size budget: if json.dumps(receipt, indent=1) exceeds about MAX_TEXT, drop the per-rep arrays (workloads[*].reps) and set "clipped": true. Clipping structuredContent to a similar budget is optional.

title: POST /receipts with Content-Length > 1 MB returns 400 without draining the body on a keep-alive connection
ref: origin/bench:worker/receipts.py handle() read_raw(1_000_000); origin/integration:worker/jobworker.py _route closes the connection only for PUT
scenario: A client sends a receipt larger than 1 MB, or a wrong Content-Length. _raw raises ValueError before reading anything, and receipts_handle turns it into 400. jobworker._route sets close_connection only when method == 'PUT' (the PR #4 fix), so the HTTP/1.1 connection stays open with the body unread. The server then parses the leftover body bytes as the next request line (garbage or desync) for that client. Also, bodies between 256 KB and 1 MB are buffered in full before being rejected with 413.
evidence: In integration jobworker._route: `if method == "PUT" and status >= 400: self.close_connection = True`. receipts.handle uses POST with `store.save(read_raw(1_000_000))`, and save() rejects anything over MAX_RECEIPT=256 KB only after the read.
fix: Call read_raw(MAX_RECEIPT + 1) so oversize bodies are rejected without buffering 1 MB. In jobworker._route, close the connection for any status >= 400 on a request with a body (POST as well as PUT), or on any 413/400 raised by a body reader.
notes: UPHELD(medium): I confirmed the path by reading the code, but I did not run anything. In origin/bench:worker/receipts.py, `handle()` calls `store.save(read_raw(1_000_000))` for POST /receipts. On origin/bench, federated.py:245 sends /receipts to `receipts_handle(receipts, method, parts, query, read_raw)`. `read_raw` is the handler's `self._raw` (passed in `_route` as `router(method, parts, parse_qs(url.query), self._body, self._raw)`). `_raw(limit)` raises ValueError("bad or too large Content-Length") before calling `rfile.read` when n < 0 or n > limit. The `except ValueError` in receipts.handle (and the one in `_route`) turns that into a 400. In origin/integration:worker/jobworker.py, `_route` sets `self.close_connection = True` only for `method == "PUT" and status >= 400`. The bench copy of `_route` does not have even that, because bench is not based on the current integration. So a POST with Content-Length over 1,000,000, or a negative one, gets its 400 while the body is still unread on an HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection (`protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"`). BaseHTTPRequestHandler then reads the leftover body bytes as the next request line. It sends a stray 400 or 414 and closes, and a client that reuses the connection can receive that stray response for its next request. Caveats that keep the severity low: the iPad's real receipts are about 20-60 KB, so this needs a misbehaving client. The same gap already exists for every POST that goes through `_body()` with more than 1 MB, so receipts adds a new instance of an existing pattern rather than a new kind of bug. The claim's second part is real but harmless. A body between 256 KB and 1 MB is read in full before `save()` raises OverflowError and returns 413. That costs at most about 1 MB of buffering and leaves the connection in sync, so the only real defect is the unread body on rejected POSTs. | fix: In integration worker/jobworker.py `_route`, close the connection on any error response to a request whose body may be unread. Replace `if method == "PUT" and status >= 400:` with `if method in ("PUT", "POST") and status >= 400:`. Or narrower: set `self.close_connection = True` inside `_raw`/`_body` just before raising the Content-Length ValueError. In receipts.handle, call `read_raw(MAX_RECEIPT + 1)` so oversize receipts are rejected before the body is read; that rejection needs the connection-close fix above too.

UPHELD(high): I could not refute the claim. The code confirms it.

1. origin/bench:worker/receipts.py `handle()` POST /receipts calls `store.save(read_raw(1_000_000))`. The wiring is in origin/bench:worker/federated.py:244-245, which routes `receipts` paths to `receipts_handle(..., read_raw)`.
2. origin/bench does not change worker/jobworker.py. `git diff integration...bench --stat` touches only federated, fleet, mcp_bridge, receipts and the tests. So the integration `Handler` applies:
   - `protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"`, so connections are keep-alive.
   - `_raw(limit)` checks `n < 0 or n > limit` and raises ValueError before `rfile.read`. A non-integer Content-Length also raises ValueError inside `int()`.
   - receipts.handle catches that ValueError and returns `(400, ...)`.
   - `_route` sets `self.close_connection = True` only when `method == "PUT" and status >= 400`.
3. Result: a POST /receipts with Content-Length over 1,000,000 gets a 400, the connection stays open, and the body is still unread. BaseHTTPRequestHandler then reads those leftover bytes as the next request line. That makes garbage requests or a desynced connection for that client.
4. A body between 256 KB and 1 MB is read into memory in full, then rejected with OverflowError (413). The test at test_fleet.py:249 (pad=300_000) shows this path works, so the only cost is the wasted read.

Severity stays low. The iPad app's receipts are about 20-60 KB, and an oversize or malformed Content-Length only breaks that one client's own connection. The same pattern already exists before this PR: `_body` on POST routes rejects n > 1 MB without reading the body or closing the connection. This branch adds one more instance of it. | fix: In integration worker/jobworker.py `_route`, change the condition `if method == "PUT" and status >= 400:` to `if method in ("PUT", "POST") and status >= 400:`. A simpler alternative is to close whenever `status >= 400` and the request had a nonzero Content-Length. This also fixes the same existing problem in `_body`. In bench worker/receipts.py, change the POST line to `store.save(read_raw(MAX_RECEIPT + 1))`. Then an oversize Content-Length is rejected before anything is read, instead of first buffering up to 1 MB.

UPHELD(medium): I confirmed this from the source. It is a real defect but a minor one: severity low, and the pattern is partly older than this branch.

Code path:
1. origin/bench adds `receipts_handle(receipts, method, parts, query, read_raw)` to `federated.make_router`. `receipts.handle` calls `store.save(read_raw(1_000_000))` for POST /receipts.
2. `jobworker.Handler._raw(limit)` reads `n = int(Content-Length)`. If `n > limit`, it raises `ValueError("bad or too large Content-Length")` before reading any bytes from `rfile`.
3. `receipts.handle` catches the ValueError and returns `(400, {...})`. A non-integer Content-Length takes the same path, because `int()` raises ValueError.
4. In origin/integration, `_route` sets `self.close_connection = True` only when `method == "PUT" and status >= 400`. The handler uses `protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"`, so after a POST it stays in keep-alive mode with the unread body still on the socket.
5. `handle_one_request` then reads the leftover body bytes as the next request line. The server sends a garbage 400 (bad request line or version) to that client, and the client's next real request on that connection is desynchronised or lost.

Bench's own copy of jobworker predates PR #4 and closes nothing for any method. Once merged, integration's PUT-only rule is what applies.

Why it is only low:
- The real client sends receipts of about 20-60 KB, so it is unlikely to exceed 1 MB.
- The callers are authenticated (bearer token), so nobody else can trigger it.
- The impact is limited to that client's own connection; there is no data loss and the server keeps running.
- The same no-drain behaviour already exists for every POST route that uses `_body` (it also raises before reading when Content-Length > 1 MB). Bench adds another instance of it; it did not introduce the pattern.

The secondary part of the claim is not a correctness bug. Bodies between 256 KB and 1 MB are read in full and then rejected with 413. Because the body is drained, the connection stays consistent; the only cost is buffering up to 1 MB. | fix: In integration's `worker/jobworker.py` `_route`, close the connection on any error response to a request that may carry a body, for example `if method in ("PUT", "POST") and status >= 400: self.close_connection = True`. For full coverage, also set `close_connection = True` in `_raw` and `_body` right before they raise for an oversize or invalid Content-Length. That also covers the non-router `do_POST` path, which calls `_body` directly. title: Receipt listing 'newest first' is wrong within the same second and for suffixes >= 10; every listing re-reads every file
scenario: Two receipts for the same model in the same second are named S-m.json then S-m-2.json. Because '.' > '-', a reverse lexicographic sort lists the OLDER S-m.json first. With 10 or more collisions, '-10' sorts below '-2'. Across models within one second, order follows the model name, not the time, so list_receipts(limit=1) can return a stale receipt. In addition, with a model filter that matches rarely, each call json-parses every stored receipt (up to 256 KB each, never deleted), so the cost of each MCP call grows without bound.
evidence: The PR's own test hedges on this: `self.assertIn(s["workloads"][0]["decode_tps"], (61.2, 70.0))`. Python: sorted(['S-m.json','S-m-2.json'], reverse=True) == ['S-m.json','S-m-2.json'].
fix: Use a zero-padded monotonic sequence in the name (e.g. stamp-<seq:04d>-model.json), or sort by (stamp, n) parsed from the name. Keep a small in-memory index of (name, model_id) built at startup and updated on save, so filtered listings skip non-matching files without reading them.
notes:
UPHELD(high): I could not refute this. I checked origin/bench:worker/receipts.py and the claim holds.

- **How files are named (save, lines 76-84):** each receipt is named `{stamp}-{model}.json`, where the stamp has one-second resolution. If that name already exists, the next one is `{stamp}-{model}-{n}.json`.
- **How listing orders them (line 97):** `list()` sorts with `sorted(self.root.glob("*.json"), reverse=True)`, and the comment there says names start with a UTC stamp. The docstring at line 8 promises "newest first".
- **Same-second collision:** `.` (0x2E) sorts after `-` (0x2D). I ran it in Python: `sorted(['S-m.json','S-m-2.json'], reverse=True)` returns `['S-m.json','S-m-2.json']`. So the older receipt comes first.
- **Ten or more collisions:** `-10` sorts below `-2` as text, so the order breaks again.
- **Different models in the same second:** they are ordered by model name, not by time.
- **The PR's own test hedges on this:** test_fleet.py:236 accepts either value with `assertIn(s["workloads"][0]["decode_tps"], (61.2, 70.0))`.
- **Effect:** list_receipts with limit=1 can return a stale receipt.
- **Cost of filtered listings:** every file is parsed before the model filter is applied (lines 100-105). Receipts are never deleted, and each can be up to MAX_RECEIPT in size. A rarely matching filter therefore reads the whole store on every call.

Severity is low. It only matters when receipts are saved within the same second, and on a single-user worker the store grows slowly. Real impact is a wrong "latest" result plus listing cost that grows linearly with the number of receipts. | fix: Sort by (stamp, n) parsed from the filename, with an unsuffixed name counting as n=1, or use a sub-second or zero-padded sequence in the name, such as `{stamp}-{seq:04d}-{model}.json`. For the cost problem, keep an in-memory index of (name, model_id) built at startup and updated on save, or put the model id in the filename and match on it, so filtered listings skip non-matching files without parsing them.

UPHELD(high): I confirmed this on origin/bench:worker/receipts.py. ReceiptStore.save names files `{stamp}-{model}.json` and uses `{stamp}-{model}-{n}.json` when the name is taken. The stamp only has one-second resolution (`%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ`).

ReceiptStore.list (line ~96) does `sorted(self.root.glob("*.json"), reverse=True)` and nothing re-sorts the result. Comparing "S-m.json" with "S-m-2.json", the first difference is '.' (0x2E) against '-' (0x2D). '.' is larger, so the reverse sort puts the older S-m.json first. With ten or more collisions, "-10" also sorts below "-9". Across models in the same second, the order follows the model name, not the write time.

No guard prevents this: there is no sequence number, no mtime sort, and no index. So limit=1 can return a receipt that is not the newest. Every listing also reads and json-parses each receipt file (up to 256 KB) until it has `limit` matches, and receipts are never deleted. A model filter that rarely matches therefore makes the cost grow linearly with the number of stored receipts.

The impact is small, so severity stays low. Same-second collisions need fast repeated bench posts, and the cost growth only matters at a large receipt count. | fix: Sort by a key parsed from the name: (stamp, n), where n is 1 when there is no suffix. Alternatively, put a zero-padded per-second sequence in the name before the model (`{stamp}-{seq:03d}-{model}.json`), and also mtime_ns as a tie-break across models. Optionally keep an in-memory index of (name, model_id), built at init and updated in save, so filtered listings skip files that cannot match.

UPHELD(high): I confirmed this on origin/bench. In worker/receipts.py, save() names the first receipt in a given second <stamp>-<model>.json and later ones <stamp>-<model>-<n>.json. list() at line 96 then sorts the names in reverse string order, assuming that puts the newest first.

That assumption fails in three ways:
1. '.' (0x2E) sorts above '-' (0x2D). Running Python on the bench names gives sorted(['20261126T000000Z-m.json','20261126T000000Z-m-2.json'], reverse=True) == ['…-m.json', '…-m-2.json'], so the older receipt comes first.
2. '-10' sorts below '-2', so with ten or more receipts in one second the order breaks again.
3. Across different models in the same second, the order follows the model name, not the time.

So list_receipts(limit=1) through mcp_bridge.t_list_receipts can return a stale receipt. The PR's own test at worker/test_fleet.py:236 hedges on this with assertIn(decode_tps, (61.2, 70.0)) instead of checking a single expected value.

The cost part also holds. With a model filter, every non-matching receipt (up to 256 KB each) is read and JSON-parsed before the filter is checked. The store never deletes receipts, so the cost of each call keeps growing.

Low severity is right: this only affects ordering and speed, with no data loss or crash. | fix: Sort with a key parsed from the name: (stamp, model, n) gives a stable order but still follows the model name within one second. To get true newest-first, put a zero-padded sequence in the name or sort by (stamp, mtime_ns). Alternatively, name every file with an explicit zero-padded counter (<stamp>-<seq:03d>-<model>.json), so plain string sorting matches creation order. To avoid parsing non-matching files on filtered listings, keep a small in-memory index of (name, model_id).

title: Merge hazard: docs/ENGINEERING-LOG.md conflicts with integration (worker code merges cleanly)
ref: trial merge of origin/bench into origin/integration
scenario: Merging PR #7 into the current integration (which includes PR #4) stops on a content conflict in docs/ENGINEERING-LOG.md. worker/fleet.py, federated.py, mcp_bridge.py and test_fleet.py auto-merge. After the conflict was set aside, all 56 worker tests passed (test_fleet, test_mcp_bridge, test_jobworker; 2 skipped). list_receipts works under integration's validate() and the receipts route is checked before /fed and the fleet routes. Open PRs #2, #3, #5 and #6 touch no worker/ or .github files.
evidence: `git merge --no-edit bench` in a --shared temp clone: 'CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in docs/ENGINEERING-LOG.md'. `python -m unittest test_fleet test_mcp_bridge test_jobworker` -> 'Ran 56 tests ... OK (skipped=2)'.
